messages.author: b756a7daa2c2aa6d
messages.subject: Re: dplyr: Oracle and MS SQL?
parts:
> In the R studio blog, you mention "adding a new backend is a matter of
> implementing a handful of S3 methods." Could you expand on this? I'm sure
> its documented somewhere, I'm just having trouble finding it. Might it just
> be something like this?
> https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/blob/master/R/src-postgres.r but for our db
> of choice?

Right, it's not documented anywhere, but it's not too hard. Here's a
quick stab at how I'd go about implementing a new backend.

# src

* Start with creating a new src to represent the backend. Assuming
we're going to create a src for mssql, you'd call it src_mssql, and
you'd follow the pattern of an existing src, eg. src-mysql.r.
Basically, all the object needs to store is information about how to
connect to the database, and it should implement a method of
brief_desc() to briefly describe the source.

* Next implement the database level methods in dbi-s3.r:
dbi_connect(), db_list_tables(), db_has_table(), db_data_type(). These
should be fairly obvious once you look at the existing
implementations.

* With these implemented you should be able to connect to a src and
get a useful description, including a list of tables. Iterate until
that works.

# tbl

* Next implement the tbl method for your data source. This will probably just be

tbl.src_mssql <- function(src, from, ...) {
tbl_sql("mssql", src = src, from = from, ...)
}

* Then implement the query related methods in dbi-s3.r: qry_fields(),
table_fields(), qry_fetch(), qry_explain(). Again, these aren't
documented, but are pretty simple and there are lots of existing code.

* Once you've done this you should be able to connect to a tbl in your
new source, and get a reasonable print out. Iterate until that works.

* If the database is not ANSI SQL compliant, you'll need to provide
methods for the sql_* methods in dbi-s3.r: sql_begin_trans(),
sql_commit(), sql_insert_into(), sql_create_indexes(), sql_analyze().

* At this point, summarise(), filter(), arrange(), mutate() etc should all work

# sql translation

* To finish off, you can add custom R -> SQL translation by providing
a method for translate_env. This function should return an object
created by sql_variant(). See existing methods for examples.

If you're familiar with how your database works, and at least one
other database that dplyr already supports, this should be reasonably
simple, and I'm happy to help if you get stuck. It's also possible
that a new database backend may need new methods - I'm also happy to
add those as needed.

Hadley

--

parts:
Hi Hadley, 

I've had a go at running the rsqlserver package, but it may not be robust enough yet to be used by dplyr. 

That said, I've been following your instructions above to try to get Oracle working using the ROracle package. 

I've managed to get src_oracle and tbl() working correctly, but have had to hack ROracle to do it.

Here are some issues I've found:
  • Oracle throws an error for statements ending  ";" when using ROracle
  • The "AS" in "SELECT id, name FROM (SELECT id, name FROM x) AS y" throws an error. The correct syntax is to omit the "AS" part when it relates to sub-queries. Here below are a few valid examples of alias names for tables and columns. 
    • SELECT id AS my_id, name AS my_name FROM (SELECT id, name FROM x) y
    • SELECT id my_id, name my_name FROM (SELECT id, name FROM x) y
    • SELECT id my_id, name my_name FROM (SELECT id, name FROM x)    
  • LIMIT doesn't work in Oracle. The equivalent is something like this:
SELECT outer.*
  FROM (SELECT ROWNUM rn, inner.*
          FROM (  SELECT e.*
                    FROM employee e
                ORDER BY hiredate) inner) outer
 WHERE outer.rn >= 5 AND outer.rn <= 10

So src_oracle() and tbl() now "work" but I've had to modify ROracle to strip out the semi-colons, AS, and LIMIT it finds in SQL statements.

What's the best way to change dplyr to get those working for real? It seems those issues are hard-coded and there isn't currently any code make the functions act differently for different tbl_xxx objects.

> Is it a requirement that there be a DBI compliant interface to the database
> in question? Is it unlikely that dplyr could use RODBC in the future?

It's not a requirement. The bigquery interface is very far from being
DBI and it works fine. As long as you can implement methods for the
functions I mentioned you should be fine. A generic ODBC connector
could also be an option.

> SELECT id my_id, name my_name FROM (SELECT id, name FROM x) y
> SELECT id my_id, name my_name FROM (SELECT id, name FROM x)

Ok, so that means dplyr needs a method for naming subqueries - I think
I'm already using the from function consistently, so it needs to be
made into a generic and added to dbi-s3.r with an appropriate name.

> LIMIT doesn't work in Oracle. The equivalent is something like this:
>
> SELECT outer.*
> FROM (SELECT ROWNUM rn, inner.*
> FROM ( SELECT e.*
> FROM employee e

> WHERE outer.rn >= 5 AND outer.rn <= 10

necessary. I using limit for (e.g.) head(tbl) but it's redundant with
the number of rows supplied to fetch. My initial thinking was this the
LIMIT would help the database optimise the query (because it would
know that it doesn't need to compute more than n rows), but I don't
think most (any?) databases actually do that optimisation.

messages.author: ca5dd90d5422193f
messages.subject: Re: dplyr: Oracle and MS SQL?
parts:
Thanks for the guidance Hadley. I'm pretty new to advanced R programming (your book has been a big help) and new to git/github as well. 

Anyway, I'm fairly certain I've ironed out the issues with Oracle and done so without (hopefully) breaking anything else. 

The main difference is the addition of sql_as() generics to name sub-queries in a manner that works in Oracle (i.e. without an "AS").

I've also changed head.tbl_sql() to use build_query(x)$fetch(n) instead of build_query(x, limit = n)$fetch() thus avoiding the use of LIMIT entirely, as per your comments. Note that I haven't removed any of the code that could work with LIMIT in SQL; just removed the need for it by changing head.table_sql().

I made a minor change to utils.r unique_name(); table name is now "W_" , instead of "_W", which did not work in Oracle. 

As you described in a previous note, the rest of the changes were pretty straightforward; just generics for OraConnection.

I don't yet have qry_explain.OraConnection() working, nor lahman_oracle(), but it looks like all of the single and binary verbs are working correctly.

we're going to create a src for mssql, you'd call it src_mssql, and
you'd follow the pattern of an existing src, eg. src-mysql.r.
Basically, all the object needs to store is information about how to
connect to the database, and it should implement a method of
brief_desc() to briefly describe the source.

* Next implement the database level methods in dbi-s3.r:
dbi_connect(), db_list_tables(), db_has_table(), db_data_type(). These
should be fairly obvious once you look at the existing
implementations.

* With these implemented you should be able to connect to a src and
get a useful description, including a list of tables. Iterate until
that works.

# tbl

* Next implement the tbl method for your data source. This will probably just be

tbl.src_mssql <- function(src, from, ...) {
  tbl_sql("mssql", src = src, from = from, ...)
}

* Then implement the query related methods in dbi-s3.r: qry_fields(),
table_fields(), qry_fetch(), qry_explain(). Again, these aren't
documented, but are pretty simple and there are lots of existing code.

* Once you've done this you should be able to connect to a tbl in your
new source, and get a reasonable print out. Iterate until that works.

* If the database is not ANSI SQL compliant, you'll need to provide
methods for the sql_* methods in dbi-s3.r: sql_begin_trans(),
sql_commit(), sql_insert_into(), sql_create_indexes(), sql_analyze().

* At this point, summarise(), filter(), arrange(), mutate() etc should all work

# sql translation

* To finish off, you can add custom R -> SQL translation by providing
a method for translate_env. This function should return an object
created by sql_variant(). See existing methods for examples.

If you're familiar with how your database works, and at least one
other database that dplyr already supports, this should be reasonably
simple, and I'm happy to help if you get stuck.  It's also possible
that a new database backend may need new methods - I'm also happy to
add those as needed.

Hadley

Hi,

after Oracle introduced ORE (Oracle R Enterprise) with their own SQL abstraction layer I don't think that Oracle is willing to do the same in dplyr. Is there any chance that dplyr will support Oracle as additional backend? I see there has been some progress made by others - would it be difficult to incorporate this work into dplyr? Is there anyone willing to co-operate on this? I would love to use my medium-level R programming skills to help and make Oracle backend part of dplyr.

Tomas

Dne pátek 28. března 2014 18:28:43 UTC+1 Einar Hjorleifsson napsal(a):

hi all

i have been tracing this thread and then some. issue is connection to oracle via dplyr. managed to set up a connection and then retrieve data following what i found on this thread and on https://github.com/datalove/dplyr/tree/oracle
something like the following works:
my_db <- src_oracle(dbname = "mar", user = "xxx",password = "xxx")
my_db
my_tbl <- tbl(my_db, "SUGSKIP")
x <- filter(my_tbl,HEITI=="Tjaldur")
collect(x)

however the listed tables in my_db only contain my own tables (like SUGSKIP). the database in question ("mar") contains myriads of other tables that are under the <schema>.<table> syntax (of which i have no write permission). a typical ROracle environment syntax that works is:
require(ROracle)
drv <- dbDriver("Oracle")
con <- dbConnect(drv,user="xxx",password="xxx",dbname="mar")
rs <- dbSendQuery(con,"select * from fish.samplingclass")
dat <- fetch(rs)

wander if the reason for not accessing the tables via dplyr is the <schema>.<table> syntax (e.g. <fish>.<samplingclass>)? and if so i would be pleased if somebody could lead me into the right directions within the dplyr framework. or am i totally off the path here.

regards,
einar

On Sunday, 9 February 2014 13:39:48 UTC, TMOD wrote:
Thanks for the guidance Hadley. I'm pretty new to advanced R programming (your book has been a big help) and new to git/github as well. 

Anyway, I'm fairly certain I've ironed out the issues with Oracle and done so without (hopefully) breaking anything else. 

The main difference is the addition of sql_as() generics to name sub-queries in a manner that works in Oracle (i.e. without an "AS").

I've also changed head.tbl_sql() to use build_query(x)$fetch(n) instead of build_query(x, limit = n)$fetch() thus avoiding the use of LIMIT entirely, as per your comments. Note that I haven't removed any of the code that could work with LIMIT in SQL; just removed the need for it by changing head.table_sql().

I made a minor change to utils.r unique_name(); table name is now "W_" , instead of "_W", which did not work in Oracle. 

As you described in a previous note, the rest of the changes were pretty straightforward; just generics for OraConnection.

I don't yet have qry_explain.OraConnection() working, nor lahman_oracle(), but it looks like all of the single and binary verbs are working correctly.




On Sat, Feb 8, 2014 at 3:29 AM, Hadley Wickham <h.wi...@gmail.com> wrote:
> That said, I've been following your instructions above to try to get Oracle
> working using the ROracle package.

Awesome, thanks!

> I've managed to get src_oracle and tbl() working correctly, but have had to
> hack ROracle to do it.
>
> Here are some issues I've found:
>
> Oracle throws an error for statements ending  ";" when using ROracle

I think that's only used in one place in dplyr
(qry_fields.DBIConnection) so it should be an easy fix.

> The "AS" in "SELECT id, name FROM (SELECT id, name FROM x) AS y" throws an
> error. The correct syntax is to omit the "AS" part when it relates to
> sub-queries. Here below are a few valid examples of alias names for tables
> and columns.
>
> SELECT id AS my_id, name AS my_name FROM (SELECT id, name FROM x) y
> SELECT id my_id, name my_name FROM (SELECT id, name FROM x) y
> SELECT id my_id, name my_name FROM (SELECT id, name FROM x)

Ok, so that means dplyr needs a method for naming subqueries - I think
I'm already using the from function consistently, so it needs to be
made into a generic and added to dbi-s3.r with an appropriate name.

> LIMIT doesn't work in Oracle. The equivalent is something like this:
>
> SELECT outer.*
>   FROM (SELECT ROWNUM rn, inner.*
>           FROM (  SELECT e.*
>                     FROM employee e
>                 ORDER BY hiredate) inner) outer
>  WHERE outer.rn >= 5 AND outer.rn <= 10

LIMIT is only used in a handful of places, and may not even be
necessary. I using limit for (e.g.) head(tbl) but it's redundant with
the number of rows supplied to fetch. My initial thinking was this the
LIMIT would help the database optimise the query (because it would
know that it doesn't need to compute more than n rows), but I don't
think most (any?) databases actually do that optimisation.

> What's the best way to change dplyr to get those working for real? It seems
> those issues are hard-coded and there isn't currently any code make the
> functions act differently for different tbl_xxx objects.

Right, it basically means adding new generics.  Do you want to have a
go? I'm happy to review pull requests as you go.

Hadley
